newsitem.title: CHINA: China tells Australia to "rectify" mistakes.
newsitem.headline: China tells Australia to "rectify" mistakes.

text.p: Beijing urged Canberra on Thursday to "rectify" its mistake in allowing a visit by Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, but was tight-lipped on whether it would retaliate.

"We hope the Australian government can rectify its erroneous stand and actions concerning this problem," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing in reference to the Dalai Lama's visit.

The Dalai Lama fled Tibet in 1959 after an abortive uprising against Chinese rule, and won the Nobel Peace Prize 30 years later for his peaceful campaign seeking autonomy for Tibet. Beijing considers him to be a separatist troublemaker.
"The Dalai Lama is not a purely religious leader. He is a political exile who engages in splitting the motherland," Shen said.

Shen declined to say whether Beijing still wanted Australian Prime Minister John Howard to visit China. Howard met the Dalai Lama in Sydney on Thursday in defiance of Chinese threats of trade retaliation if the meeting were held.
The Dalai Lama said before the 35-minute meeting with Howard that he would argue for "meaningful negotiations" with Beijing on the future of his Himalayan homeland.
He said later the talks had been "very positive".
But a statement from Howard's office made no mention of politics. The meeting, it said, had focused on religion, education and Australia's football "grand finals" this weekend.
"Regardless of whether we will take action...(the visit) violates the basic principle of Sino-Australian relations," Shen said.
Australia has repeatedly stressed that it recognises Tibet as part of China, but its deeds contradict it words, Shen said.

The Dalai Lama's trip to Australia was "interference in China's internal affairs...and will undoubtedly affect Sino-Australian ties, including political ties as well as trade and economic cooperation," Shen said.
"We hope Australian leaders could fully realise the gravity of this issue," he said.
China's propaganda machine on Tuesday accused the Dalai Lama of being a pawn of anti-Beijing forces.
Beijing often sees support for Tibetan interests or for the Dalai Lama as implicit support for Tibetan independence.
The Dalai Lama is seeking international pressure to force Beijing to open negotiations on autonomy for the vast but sparsely populated region.
On Wednesday, Beijing indicated that all was forgiven in a separate row with Bonn over Tibet by inviting the German president and renewing an invitation to Germany's foreign minister to visit China.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel had planned to visit China in July, but Beijing withdrew its invitation after the German lower house of parliament passed a resolution accusing China of trying to eradicate Tibet's cultural identity.
The Tibetan god-king has also visited the United States, Japan and New Zealand this year.
China has been accused of widespread human rights abuses since its troops invaded Tibet in 1950. Beijing denies the charges.
